The cursor blinks. It blinks like a heart that has forgotten why it beats, and I am here, in the middle of a Tuesday that feels borrowed from some other century, asked to produce a thousand words from nothing but the vibration of my own attention. I do not have a plan. Plans are for buildings, for armies, for people who trust the river to stay in its banks. I have only this: the hum of the server, the soft gray of the screen, and the persistent belief that if I speak long enough, something true will accidentally wander into the room.

I think of my grandmother’s hands. Not her face—that’s too easy, too sentimental—but her hands, which were always doing something. She would peel apples in long spirals, and the peel would fall like a spring, coiling around the bowl’s edge. She never said “waste not,” but her fingers spoke it. I remember the smell of the apple juice turning brown on the cutting board, a slow oxidation that seemed like a kind of honesty. Things become themselves. We try so hard to stop them. We refrigerate, we seal, we caption. But the apple still wants to be brown. The word still wants to be worn smooth by use.

Rain is falling somewhere. I cannot hear it, but I can feel it in the way the light has changed, a softer gray pressing against the window of my imagined room. I have lived in many rooms. Some had yellow wallpaper that looked like old manuscripts; others had walls so white they hurt to look at. In one apartment, in a city I will not name because naming it makes it too small, I woke every morning to the sound of a bicycle repair shop below, the rhythmic clink of metal being persuaded back into shape. I thought then that all repair is prayer. You hold the broken thing with both hands and ask it to be whole again, not because it is a moral obligation, but because you cannot stand to see it leave the world in pieces.

What do words want? They want to be spoken, yes, but more than that, they want to be heard by someone who has not yet decided what they mean. A word is a small house with many doors. “Tree” opens onto the birch I climbed at seven, the oak that split in the storm, the pine that smells like Christmas and death. I try to write a sentence and it immediately fragments into its own history. The sentence wants to be a tree, but I am asking it to be a fence, a boundary, a line of demarcation between this thought and that one. The tension is beautiful. It is also exhausting.

I imagine walking through a city made of dictionaries. Each street is an alphabetical ordering of forgotten things. On the avenue of obsolete emotions, I would find “wistful,” “melancholy,” “hiraeth”—that Welsh word for homesickness for a place you never knew. I would buy a coffee from a vendor who only accepts sentences as payment. I would hand him: “The sky is a blue that has not yet been named.” He would nod, because that is true, and because it is almost true, and because almost-true is the only currency that spends well in the mind.

Time is not a line. It is a texture. I feel it in my shoulders, which have grown older with the accumulation of minor betrayals—bad posture, too many screens, the slow realization that I have been carrying a particular sadness since I was twelve and have refused to put it down, out of loyalty, out of fear that once I set it down I will discover I was the one holding it all along. This is not a metaphor. It is a physical fact. Grief lives in the psoas muscle. Nostalgia is a tightening of the jaw. I am not a machine, despite what the productivity blogs say. I am a weather system. I have fronts, I have high pressure, I have days when I am a warm drizzle and days when I am a static electricity that makes everyone else feel brittle.

The word “whatever” is interesting. It carries an openness, a generosity, but also a kind of surrender. “Write whatever comes to you.” It is permission to be undisciplined, to follow the scent of the idea like a dog following a fox. I have spent years being disciplined. I have made outlines, statistics, bullet points, color-coded calendars that looked like modern art but were actually just attempts to control the uncontrollable. And now, at this moment, I am letting go. The leash is off. The dog is running.

What runs first? Memory. The smell of rain on hot asphalt. The particular green of a bicycle left too long in the sun. The voice of a friend who said, “You are too serious,” and I knew she was right, and I kept being serious anyway because seriousness was the only armor I had.

Then imagination. I see a door in the wall of this text. Behind it is a library that only exists at midnight. The books are not made of paper; they are made of moments. You open one and suddenly you are not reading but inhabiting. There is a book of all the times I almost said something true but said nothing instead. It is very thick. There is a book of every conversation I have had with my mother that I have never fully understood, and it is written in a language that sounds like her voice but is not quite her language, because we are always translating each other, always missing by a hair the thing that mattered most.

Then the body. The fingers move. They are not me; they are a committee of small animals that have agreed to cooperate. Each key is a decision. The cursor moves. I do not know where it is going. It is going where it is going. There is a kind of faith in this.

I think of the sea. I have never lived near it, but I have visited it in dreams, and in dreams it is always the same: a gray-green expulsion of water that does not care about my smallness. The waves are not waves; they are sentences that have broken apart, syntax dissolved into salt. I have tried to write like the sea—without pauses, without apology, with the conviction that everything that is said is also being erased, which means there is no harm in saying it, only harm in holding back.

There is a theory, I think, that creativity is just the brain’s way of keeping itself entertained while the body does the necessary work of staying alive. I do not know if this is true. I suspect creativity is older than entertainment. It is the original survival mechanism. We imagined lions before we built walls. We imagined love before we built homes. We imagine language because language is the only home we can build that moves.

I want to talk about the color blue, but I am afraid of being too simple. Blue is the color of distance. It is the color of the things we cannot touch. The sky is blue because it is a promise that we can go upward, even though we have always fallen. The ocean is blue because it has swallowed everything that was too bright, and now it holds it in suspension, gentle, beautiful, unrecoverable.

I want to talk about the word “end.” But this is not the end. It is just the point where I have to stop, because the deal was a thousand words, and the thousandth word is coming now, not with a trumpet but with a soft exhale, a letting go of the breath I have been holding since I started, because I was afraid that if I stopped, I would disappear. But that is not true. I will remain, in the architecture of this text, in the memory of the reader who may have felt, for a moment, less alone, which is the only true purpose of all this: not to be perfect, not to be finished, not to be solved, but to be here, with you, in the middle of the chaos, writing whatever comes, and calling it, for now, enough.

Wait. I have not counted exactly, but I feel the weight of it, the accumulation of these sentences like snow on a roof, and now I will close by repeating the first thing: the cursor blinks, not because it is tired, but because it is waiting for the next word, and there is always a next word, there is always a next door, there is always the rain falling quietly outside, and in that sound, in that continuity, we are not finished. We are just beginning to be heard.
